conventions.convention: Linear margins are y_i〈w,x_i〉, with no intercept; the hard-margin objective is one half the squared Euclidean norm under margins at least one.

A global Clarke flow is locally absolutely continuous and satisfies the negative subdifferential inclusion almost everywhere. The arc chain rule requires equality for every Clarke subgradient at almost every time and is an additional hypothesis.
Parameter homogeneity uses positive scaling and a common degree L>0. Exponential empirical risk is a sum, without division by sample size.

For lower constraints q_i≥1, KKT stationarity is θ=Σλ_i h_i with λ_i≥0. MFCQ requires positive pairing with every subgradient of every active margin. Approximate complementarity is the aggregate nonnegative error Σλ_i(q_i−1).
Countable Choice is assumed only for the almost-everywhere feature-array conclusion; the discrete all-data comparison and homogeneous-flow arguments claim no additional choice principle.

load_bearing.statement: For locally Lipschitz F, the defined Clarke subdifferential is nonempty compact convex, equals the closed convex hull of limiting ordinary gradients, has support function F°(x;v), is locally bounded with closed graph, and has upper-semicontinuous support functions in x for fixed v.

For finite strictly separable vectors in R^d and any η>0, there is a finite orthogonal iterated-log comparison hierarchy, starting with the unique hard-margin vector and having at most d levels, whose margins diverge and whose discrete gradient-descent defects are absolutely summable for each of the exponential and logistic empirical losses. Simultaneously positive first-stage active dual coefficients give a single level.
For locally Lipschitz q:R^d→R positively homogeneous of degree L>0, every θ≠0 and h∈∂°q(θ) satisfy 〈θ,h〉=Lq(θ), and ∂°q(cθ)=c^(L−1)∂°q(θ) for c>0.

For finitely many locally Lipschitz sample margins admitting the Clarke arc chain rule, the Clarke subdifferential of their summed exponential risk is contained in the corresponding negative weighted sum of margin subdifferentials. The arc derivative has the stated weighted pairing, and along negative Clarke flow it equals minus the squared speed almost everywhere.

For finite locally Lipschitz common-degree positively homogeneous margins admitting the Clarke arc chain rule, a global exponential-risk Clarke flow whose loss is below one has this property: every normalized-direction limit point has positive minimum margin, and its unit-minimum-margin rescaling has nearby feasible (ε,ε)-approximate Clarke KKT points for every ε>0.
For finite locally Lipschitz margins, a feasible MFCQ point is Clarke KKT if, for every ε>0, a feasible (ε,ε)-approximate Clarke KKT point exists within distance ε.

published_dependencies.used_for: The fixed-step Euclidean update convention in the least-squares and separable-loss theorems.
Diagonalizing the normal matrix and bounding the symmetric averaged Hessian in the nonexpansive comparison.
Identification of the minimum-norm least-squares solution.
Normal-equation characterization and the kernel description of all least-squares minimizers.
Finite-dimensional compactness, attainment, boundedness on spheres and balls, and compact witness intersections.
Nonnegative representations of hard-margin vectors by active constraints, including recursively projected problems.
The subdifferential finite-sum inclusion and the local Fritz-John/KKT separation argument.
The explicit assumption inherited by the polynomial-null-set argument for the almost-everywhere residual clause.

concerns.concern: The Definition asserts: “For locally Lipschitz F, this is a nonempty compact convex set and is equivalently the closed convex hull of all limits of ordinary gradients”; it additionally asserts the support-function identity, local boundedness, closed graph and upper semicontinuity. The carrier has deps: [], justified_by: [], and no proof. These are mathematical theorems about the preceding limsup-based definition, rather than defining conventions. In particular, the limiting-gradient characterization requires substantial nonsmooth-analysis support and is used explicitly by the Euler lemma and exponential-risk chain-rule lemma; closed graph and upper semicontinuity support the approximate-KKT limit proof. The statements are standard, but the required local proof or proved supplier is absent. The cited external literature does not discharge the repository's local-proof requirement.

alerts.finding: The published Definition contains inline links in its opening mathematical description: “with the convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; differentiability is the Fréchet condition of [[def-real-frechet-derivative-on-real-and-complex-matrix-spaces]]”. It also links [[lem-armijo-backtracking-terminates-for-strict-descent-directions]] before the Definition ends. These interrupt the complete defining section, contrary to the required immediately following Definition references section.

The published Definition ends with “Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.” Both hyperlinks occur inside the defining section rather than an immediately following Definition references section, violating the uninterrupted-definition rule.

The published Statement concludes “Thus a hyperplane strictly separates x from C ([[def-supporting-hyperplane-to-a-convex-set]]).” The wikilink remains inside the Statement and no immediately following Statement references section carries it, violating the uninterrupted-statement rule.

seams_checked.note: Read both page carriers and the supplier's recurrence algorithm and gradient-formula theorem. The supplier restricts ordinary derivatives to C1 maps or fixed strict branches, includes the initial-state contribution and T=0, and asserts no floating-point guarantee. The consumer page makes only a prerequisite declaration; its nonsmooth results independently require the Clarke arc chain rule and do not claim that backpropagation supplies classical derivatives at branch boundaries.
